q: Market supply at a given price is the:
correctAnswer: Sum of the quantities all sellers are willing and able to offer.
distractors: Quantity supplied by the single largest seller at that price.
Average quantity each seller plans to produce at that price.
Total quantity buyers are willing and able to purchase at that price.
commonError: Confusing market supply with one firm’s supply or with demand.
feedback: Market supply horizontally adds the quantities supplied by every seller at each price.
options: Sum of the quantities all sellers are willing and able to offer.
Quantity supplied by the single largest seller at that price.
Average quantity each seller plans to produce at that price.
Total quantity buyers are willing and able to purchase at that price.

q: The government begins paying producers a subsidy for every unit sold. What happens to market supply, other things equal?
correctAnswer: Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
distractors: Supply shifts left because the subsidy increases firms’ effective production cost.
Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because only the market price changed.
Demand shifts right because the payment is received directly by buyers.
commonError: Treating a producer subsidy as a movement along supply or a demand shifter.
feedback: A per-unit producer subsidy raises the return from supplying each unit and shifts supply right.
options: Supply shifts left because the subsidy increases firms’ effective production cost.
Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because only the market price changed.
Demand shifts right because the payment is received directly by buyers.

q: Workers accept lower wages, but producers also expect the product’s future price to rise and hold inventory for later sale. What can be concluded about current supply?
correctAnswer: The net direction is uncertain because the two changes push current supply in opposite directions.
distractors: Current supply must rise because the wage reduction always dominates firms’ expectations.
Current supply must fall because expected future prices always outweigh current production cost.
Only quantity supplied changes because neither event can shift the current supply curve.
commonError: Using only one supply shifter when several operate at once.
feedback: Lower wages shift supply right, while holding inventory for a higher future price shifts current supply left. The net direction depends on their relative size.
options: Current supply must rise because the wage reduction always dominates firms’ expectations.
Current supply must fall because expected future prices always outweigh current production cost.
The net direction is uncertain because the two changes push current supply in opposite directions.
Only quantity supplied changes because neither event can shift the current supply curve.

q: A new machine lowers unit production cost, while a new per-unit environmental fee raises cost. Which conclusion about supply is justified without knowing the size of each change?
correctAnswer: The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.
distractors: Supply must shift right because new technology always dominates any policy cost.
Supply must shift left because any per-unit fee always overwhelms technology.
The supply curve cannot shift whenever two opposing events occur at the same time.
commonError: Assuming one opposing supply shifter automatically dominates the other.
feedback: Technology pushes supply right and the per-unit fee pushes it left. Magnitudes are needed to determine the net shift.
options: Supply must shift right because new technology always dominates any policy cost.
Supply must shift left because any per-unit fee always overwhelms technology.
The supply curve cannot shift whenever two opposing events occur at the same time.
The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.

q: Twenty new firms enter a market, but an essential input becomes more expensive for every firm. What is the most careful conclusion about market supply?
correctAnswer: Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, making the net effect uncertain.
distractors: Market supply must rise because the increase in sellers always dominates higher costs.
Market supply must fall because input costs always dominate changes in firm entry.
Neither event changes market supply because the product’s own price stayed fixed.
commonError: Ignoring an offsetting change in the number of sellers or input costs.
feedback: More sellers expand market supply, while higher input costs reduce it. The final direction depends on relative magnitudes.
options: Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, making the net effect uncertain.
Market supply must rise because the increase in sellers always dominates higher costs.
Market supply must fall because input costs always dominate changes in firm entry.
Neither event changes market supply because the product’s own price stayed fixed.

q: Demand rises and the market price increases. Firms respond by producing more with the same technology, input prices, and number of sellers. Which statement is correct?
correctAnswer: Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
distractors: Supply shifts right because firms produce more.
Supply shifts left because the product is now more expensive.
Both supply and quantity supplied must increase.
commonError: Calling a price-induced movement along supply an increase in supply.
feedback: A change in the good’s own price changes quantity supplied. The supply curve shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.
options: Supply shifts right because firms produce more.
Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
Supply shifts left because the product is now more expensive.
Both supply and quantity supplied must increase.

q: At a price of $30, three sellers offer 12, 18, and 25 units. What is market quantity supplied at that price?
correctAnswer: 55 units.
distractors: 25 units.
30 units.
45 units.
commonError: Using the largest or average firm quantity instead of summing quantities.
feedback: Market quantity supplied is the horizontal sum: 12 + 18 + 25 = 55 units.
options: 25 units.
30 units.
55 units.
45 units.

q: A market has 80 identical firms, each supplying 6 units at a price of $10. If 20 firms exit and each remaining firm’s supply is unchanged, market quantity supplied becomes:
correctAnswer: 360 units.
distractors: 120 units.
480 units.
600 units.
commonError: Forgetting that market supply depends on the number of active sellers.
feedback: Sixty firms remain, so market quantity supplied is 60 × 6 = 360 units.
options: 120 units.
480 units.
600 units.
360 units.

q: A per-unit input cost falls by $4, but a new per-unit tax raises cost by $6. Holding other determinants fixed, what is the likely supply effect?
correctAnswer: Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
distractors: Supply shifts right because any input-cost decline dominates a tax.
Supply is unchanged because the two policies offset exactly.
Only quantity supplied falls along the same curve.
commonError: Treating unequal per-unit cost changes as if they cancel.
feedback: The combined change raises marginal cost by $2 per unit, reducing supply at each price.
options: Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
Supply shifts right because any input-cost decline dominates a tax.
Supply is unchanged because the two policies offset exactly.
Only quantity supplied falls along the same curve.

q: Producers expect a temporary price spike next month and can store the product cheaply. What pattern is most plausible?
correctAnswer: Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
distractors: Current and future supply both rise because a higher expected price makes all production more profitable.
Current supply rises as firms rush to sell before the spike, while future supply falls afterward.
Only current quantity supplied changes because expected future prices never shift supply.
commonError: Applying future price expectations in the wrong time direction.
feedback: When storage is feasible, a higher expected future price can reduce current supply and increase supply when the stored goods are later sold.
options: Current and future supply both rise because a higher expected price makes all production more profitable.
Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
Current supply rises as firms rush to sell before the spike, while future supply falls afterward.
Only current quantity supplied changes because expected future prices never shift supply.

q: A surge in demand raises the equilibrium price. Firms expand output, and new firms later enter the industry. Which sequence is correct?
correctAnswer: First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
distractors: First supply shifts right; later quantity supplied falls along the curve.
Both responses are movements along the original supply curve.
Both responses are supply shifts caused by the good’s own price.
commonError: Treating immediate output response and later firm entry as the same kind of change.
feedback: The higher price first causes a movement along supply. Entry is a nonprice determinant that later shifts market supply right.
options: First supply shifts right; later quantity supplied falls along the curve.
Both responses are movements along the original supply curve.
First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
Both responses are supply shifts caused by the good’s own price.

q: A drought reduces crop yields, while the market price of the crop rises because demand is unchanged. What is the best description?
correctAnswer: Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.
distractors: Supply shifts right because the higher equilibrium price encourages more production after the drought.
Quantity supplied falls along the original supply curve while the curve itself remains unchanged.
Demand shifts left because the drought changes buyer preferences rather than production conditions.
commonError: Using the higher equilibrium price as evidence of an increase in supply.
feedback: The drought is a supply shifter. The resulting higher price determines the quantity supplied on the new, left-shifted curve.
options: Supply shifts right because the higher equilibrium price encourages more production after the drought.
Quantity supplied falls along the original supply curve while the curve itself remains unchanged.
Demand shifts left because the drought changes buyer preferences rather than production conditions.
Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.

q: At one price, Firm A supplies 8 units and Firm B supplies 11 units. Market quantity supplied is:
correctAnswer: 19 units.
distractors: 8 units.
9.5 units.
11 units.
commonError: Averaging firm quantities instead of adding them.
feedback: Market supply adds each seller’s quantity: 8 + 11 = 19.

8 units.
9.5 units.
11 units.

q: The price of oranges rises, and growers offer more oranges while all nonprice determinants stay fixed. This is:
correctAnswer: An increase in quantity supplied.

feedback: A higher own price causes movement up the existing supply curve.
options: An increase in supply.
An increase in quantity supplied.
A decrease in supply.
A decrease in quantity supplied.

q: The price of an important input falls. What happens to supply, other things equal?
correctAnswer: Supply shifts right.
distractors: Supply shifts left.
Quantity supplied falls along the curve.

feedback: Lower input cost makes production profitable at more output levels, shifting supply right.
options: Supply shifts left.
Quantity supplied falls along the curve.
Supply shifts right.
Demand shifts right.

q: A subsidy lowers marginal cost by $3 per unit, while a regulation raises marginal cost by $3 per unit. What happens to supply if those are the only changes?
correctAnswer: The two per-unit effects offset, so supply is unchanged.
distractors: Supply shifts right because subsidies always dominate regulations.
Supply shifts left because regulations always dominate subsidies.
Quantity supplied must rise along the original curve.
commonError: Assuming the label of a policy matters more than its net marginal-cost effect.
feedback: Equal and opposite per-unit cost changes leave marginal cost, and therefore supply, unchanged.
options: Supply shifts right because subsidies always dominate regulations.
Supply shifts left because regulations always dominate subsidies.
Quantity supplied must rise along the original curve.

q: Four identical firms each supply 15 units at the current price. One firm exits and the remaining firms do not change output. Market quantity supplied becomes:
correctAnswer: 45 units.
distractors: 15 units.
30 units.
60 units.
commonError: Failing to remove the exiting firm’s quantity from market supply.

15 units.
30 units.
60 units.

q: Technology improves while the expected future selling price rises sharply and firms store current output. What is the strongest conclusion about current supply?
correctAnswer: The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
distractors: Current supply must increase because technology improved.
Current supply must decrease because expectations always dominate technology.

commonError: Declaring a net shift when opposing determinants are not quantified.
feedback: Better technology shifts supply right, while withholding output for future sale shifts current supply left.
options: Current supply must increase because technology improved.
The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
Current supply must decrease because expectations always dominate technology.
Only quantity supplied changes because both events concern production.

q: An economy produces exactly the same quantities of every final good in two years, but current prices change. Using fixed base-year prices, which statement must be true?
correctAnswer: Real GDP is unchanged.
distractors: Nominal GDP is unchanged.
The GDP deflator must equal 100 in both years.
Real GDP must rise because some current prices changed.
commonError: Treating current-price changes as changes in real output.
feedback: With quantities unchanged, valuing both years at the same base-year prices leaves real GDP unchanged.
options: Nominal GDP is unchanged.
The GDP deflator must equal 100 in both years.
Real GDP is unchanged.

q: Why is real GDP generally preferred to nominal GDP when comparing production across years?
correctAnswer: It holds prices constant so the comparison focuses on changes in output.
distractors: It includes only goods and services purchased by the government.
It values every year’s output using that year’s current market prices.
It guarantees that measured production rises from one year to the next.
commonError: Assuming nominal values isolate changes in physical production.
feedback: Real GDP uses constant prices to separate changes in quantities from changes in the price level.
options: It includes only goods and services purchased by the government.
It values every year’s output using that year’s current market prices.
It guarantees that measured production rises from one year to the next.
It holds prices constant so the comparison focuses on changes in output.

q: Two years have the same nominal GDP, but the second year has a higher GDP deflator. Which year has higher real GDP?
correctAnswer: The first year.
distractors: The second year.
They must have equal real GDP.
The answer depends only on population.
commonError: Assuming equal nominal GDP implies equal real output despite different price levels.
feedback: Real GDP equals nominal GDP divided by the price index. With equal nominal GDP, the year with the lower deflator has higher real GDP.
options: The first year.
The second year.
They must have equal real GDP.

q: Nominal GDP falls 2 percent while the GDP deflator falls 5 percent. What is the best approximate conclusion?
correctAnswer: Real GDP rises about 3 percent.
distractors: Real GDP falls about 7 percent.
Real GDP falls about 3 percent.
Real GDP is unchanged.
commonError: Adding nominal and price changes instead of separating them.
feedback: Approximate real GDP growth equals nominal GDP growth minus inflation in the deflator: −2% − (−5%) = about 3%.
options: Real GDP falls about 7 percent.
Real GDP rises about 3 percent.
Real GDP falls about 3 percent.
Real GDP is unchanged.

q: Base-year prices are $4 for books and $10 for meals. This year the economy produces 120 books and 30 meals. What is this year’s real GDP?
commonError: Using current prices or adding quantities without base-year valuation.
feedback: Real GDP uses base-year prices: (120 × $4) + (30 × $10) = $780.

q: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?
correctAnswer: The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
distractors: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.
Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
commonError: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.
feedback: Demand changes can move the economy along a given SRPC; supply shocks alter the inflation-unemployment relationship and shift the SRPC.
options: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.
Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.

q: Aggregate demand contracts unexpectedly while expected inflation is initially fixed. What short-run Phillips-curve movement is most likely?
correctAnswer: Toward lower inflation and higher unemployment.
distractors: Toward higher inflation and lower unemployment.
The entire SRPC shifts up-right immediately.
Unemployment stays fixed at the natural rate in the short run.
commonError: Confusing a demand-driven movement along the SRPC with a shift of the curve.
feedback: An unexpected demand contraction moves the economy down and right along the current SRPC.
options: Toward lower inflation and higher unemployment.
Toward higher inflation and lower unemployment.
The entire SRPC shifts up-right immediately.
Unemployment stays fixed at the natural rate in the short run.

q: Why can improved public health support long-run economic growth?
correctAnswer: Healthier workers can be more productive and miss fewer workdays.

Healthier workers can be more productive and miss fewer workdays.
It removes scarcity by preventing workers from ever becoming ill.

q: Which measure is generally more useful than total real GDP for comparing average material living standards across countries of different sizes?

The population growth rate alone.

The current price level, meaning higher prices for the same output.

q: If real GDP grows 2 percent and population grows 3 percent, real GDP per person will approximately:

Rise 5 percent.

options: Rise 1 percent.
Fall 1 percent.
Rise 5 percent.

It falls from $30,000 to about $28,571 as population increases.

options: Frictional unemployment caused by normal job search.
